meaning: Expresses the speaker's strong conviction based on facts: “must be ..., no doubt ...”. Written language.
connection: Noun／な-adj. stem／verb・い-adj. plain form + に相違ない

senses.label: Confident conclusion
senses.meaning: Based on evidence or experience, the speaker concludes that something must be so. It sounds stiffer and more formal than 「〜に違いない」. Common in writing, academic papers, news, and novels.
senses.connection: Noun・な-adj. stem + に相違ない; verb・い-adj. plain form + に相違ない; often paired with 「きっと」 or 「〜から見て」
examples: Judging from these fingerprints, the culprit must be that man.
Judging from his expression, he must be hiding something.
Since it sold this well, it must have made a considerable profit.

senses.label: Polite and other forms
senses.meaning: Polite forms are 「に相違ありません」 and 「に相違ございません」. For a past conclusion, use 「に相違なかった」. An old-fashioned variant is 「に相違あるまい」.
senses.connection: 〜に相違ありません／に相違なかった／に相違なく、〜
examples: This is without doubt my father's handwriting.
She must have been deeply hurt at the time.

notes: Almost never used in everyday conversation. In speech, 「〜に違いない」 or 「きっと〜だ」 is enough.
It expresses the speaker's own conviction. It isn't used to report someone else's guess.
「上記のとおり相違ありません」 at the end of an application form means “I certify that the above is true.” Here 「相違」 is a noun meaning “discrepancy”, so this is a different expression.

daily.title: Reading a mystery novel
daily.description: Common when a detective names the culprit from the clues.
daily.example: The culprit must be someone who knows this household well.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: The narrator draws a conclusion about a historical artifact.
daily.example: This mural must have been painted by ancient people.

work.title: Writing a report or paper
work.description: Drawing a firm conclusion from data.
work.example: This result must be due to the effects of the new system.

work.title: Testifying in court
work.description: A witness formally confirms a fact.
work.example: This signature is without doubt the person's own.

etymology: 「相違」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “difference, discrepancy”. 「〜に相違ない」 literally means “there is no difference from ...”, hence “it must be ...”. It has the same structure as 「〜に違いない」, just with a stiffer Sino-Japanese word.

similar.title: 〜に違いない
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「に違いない」 works in both speech and writing; 「に相違ない」 is only for writing or formal situations and sounds harder.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 「はずだ」 is a logical inference: “it should be, by reason or common sense”. 「に相違ない」 stresses the speaker's subjective conviction.

similar.title: 〜に決まっている
similar.explanation: 「に決まっている」 is conversational and sounds dogmatic: “it's obviously ..., no question”. 「に相違ない」 is a calm, written judgment.

meaning: Written language. Gives a reason (“due to ...”), a rate per unit (“per ...”), or works as a formal version of 「について」.

senses.label: Reason
senses.meaning: States a situation as the reason. Common in notices, announcements, and signs. Formal and objective, like “due to ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + につき; common in 「工事中につき」, 「定休日につき」, 「売り切れにつき」
examples: Due to construction, this road is closed.
We are closed today, as it is our regular holiday.
Sales have ended because the item is sold out.

senses.label: Per ...
senses.meaning: Shows allocation per unit: “per one ..., (so much)”. Similar to 「〜当たり」. Often used in rules about fees or purchase limits.
senses.connection: Counter・noun + につき + amount; e.g. 「一人につき」, 「1時間につき」
examples: The participation fee is 3,000 yen per person.
Parking is 500 yen per hour.
There is a limit of two items per customer.

senses.label: About / regarding
senses.meaning: A written, formal version of 「について」. Common in meetings and documents. The polite form is 「につきまして」.
senses.connection: Noun + につき／につきまして
examples: Please let us hear your opinion regarding this matter.
We will contact you about the schedule at a later date.

notes: When it gives a reason, it only follows nouns and is mostly found in notices. In everyday speech, people say 「〜なので」 or 「〜だから」.
The 「つく」 in 「目につく」, 「身につく」, and 「席につく」 is an ordinary verb, not this grammar point.
「〜につきまして」 is the polite form of 「〜について」 and is common in business.

daily.title: A notice on a shop door
daily.description: Seeing a notice posted on a shop's door.
daily.example: We are reserved for a private event today, so we cannot serve other customers.

daily.title: Purchase limit at the supermarket
daily.description: A clerk reminds customers of the limit.
daily.example: Eggs are limited to one pack per customer.

daily.title: Roadwork
daily.description: Seeing a construction sign by the road.
daily.example: We apologize for the inconvenience during construction.

work.title: Holiday closure notice
work.description: A company sends customers a notice about the year-end closure.
work.example: For the New Year holidays, we will be closed from December 29.

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: The chair introduces the next agenda item.
work.example: Regarding the next item on the agenda, the person in charge will explain.

etymology: Made of the particle 「に」 plus 「つき」, the stem of the verb 「付く（つく）」 “to attach”. The original sense is “attached to ...”. From “attached to a matter” it developed into “as for ...”, “because of ...”, and “per ...”. It can be written 「に付き」, but kana is usual today.

similar.title: 〜について
similar.explanation: Both can mean “about”. 「について」 is general; 「につき」 is more written and formal, mainly for official documents and meetings.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Both can give a reason. 「ため」 can follow nouns and verb clauses; 「につき」 only follows nouns and is mostly used in notices.

similar.title: 〜当たり (per)
similar.explanation: Both mean “per ...”. 「当たり」 is common for statistics and averages (「一人当たりの所得」 “income per person”); 「につき」 is mostly for rules about fees and allocation.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: 「ごとに」 stresses repetition: “every time ..., ...”. 「につき」 stresses a rate calculated per unit.

meaning: Whenever something happens, a certain feeling naturally arises. The pattern 「〜につけ〜につけ」 also means “whether ... or ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form／い-adj. dictionary form／noun + につけ(て)

senses.label: Whenever ...
senses.meaning: Every time you see, hear, or think of something, a feeling or memory naturally comes up. The second half is usually a feeling or recollection, with an emotional, reflective tone.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + につけ(て); common in 「〜を見るにつけ」, 「〜を聞くにつけ」, 「〜を思うにつけ」
examples: Whenever I see this photo, I'm reminded of my hometown.
Whenever I hear about his success, it makes me happy.
Every time I see my child's sleeping face, I want to try harder.

senses.label: Whether ... or ...
senses.meaning: 「AにつけBにつけ」 pairs two opposite words: “whether A or B, ...”. Mostly fixed pairs.
senses.connection: い-adj.・verb dictionary form + につけ + opposite word + につけ; e.g. 「いいにつけ悪いにつけ」
examples: For better or worse, he is always the center of attention.
Whether I'm happy or sad, I call my mother.

senses.label: At every opportunity
senses.meaning: The set phrase 「何かにつけ(て)」 means “at every turn, at the slightest excuse”. 「何事につけ」 means “in everything, whatever it is”.
senses.connection: 何かにつけ(て)／何事につけ(て)
examples: My mother-in-law complains to me at every turn.
He judges everything carefully, whatever it is.
My senior colleague always gives me advice whenever something comes up.

notes: In meaning 1, the second half is usually a naturally arising feeling or association, not the speaker's deliberate action (✕「見るにつけ、電話しよう」).
Don't confuse it with the verb 「つける」 in 「身につける」 or 「醤油につける」.
More written than 「〜たびに」, with a reflective, emotional tone.

daily.title: Looking through an old album
daily.description: Reflecting while looking at old photos with family.
daily.example: Whenever I look at old photos, I feel the passage of time.

daily.title: Complaining
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend about your father's love of old stories.
daily.example: My father brings up the old days at every opportunity.

daily.title: Following disaster news
daily.description: Feelings after watching news from a disaster area.
daily.example: Whenever I hear news from the disaster area, my heart aches.

work.title: Farewell party speech
work.description: A manager looks back on working with the team.
work.example: Whenever I see how much you've all grown, it makes me very happy.

work.title: Recommending a colleague
work.description: Introducing a reliable colleague to your boss.
work.example: He approaches everything with a strong sense of responsibility.

etymology: Made of the particle 「に」 plus the stem of the verb 「付ける（つける）」 “to attach”. The original sense is “attaching to ...”, which became “when connected to something”, and then “whenever ...”. It can be written 「に付け」, but kana is usual.

similar.title: 〜たびに
similar.explanation: Both mean “every time ...”. 「たびに」 is objective repetition, and any result can follow; after 「につけ」, the second half is usually a feeling or association, and it is more written.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: 「ごとに」 stresses regular repetition by unit or count; 「につけ」 is only for things that trigger feelings.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ
similar.explanation: Both can mean “whether A or B”. 「にしろ〜にしろ」 works with all kinds of contrasting items; 「につけ〜につけ」 is mostly used in fixed pairs.

meaning: As one thing changes or happens, something else changes or happens along with it. Written language, common in news and official documents.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + に伴って (に伴い／に伴う + noun)

senses.label: Change along with ...
senses.meaning: When the first part changes, the second changes with it. Both parts are words of change (増える, 進む, 高まる, etc.). Close to 「につれて」, but more formal.
senses.connection: Noun of change・verb dictionary form + に伴って; common in 「〜の増加に伴って」, 「〜化に伴って」
examples: As the population grew, housing became scarce.
As the economy developed, living standards rose too.
With the aging of society, medical costs keep rising.

senses.label: Happening as a result of ...
senses.meaning: The first part is an event, and the second is a result or measure that comes with it: “due to ..., in connection with ...”. Common in notices and news.
senses.connection: Noun + に伴い、〜; common in 「移転に伴い」, 「工事に伴い」, 「〜の接近に伴い」
examples: With the relocation of our office, our phone number will change.
As the typhoon approaches, transportation is being disrupted.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「Aに伴うB」 means “B that comes with A”. Used to modify a noun.
senses.connection: Noun + に伴う + noun
examples: Please watch out for tsunamis caused by the earthquake.
Prices continue to rise due to the weak yen.

notes: In formal written polite style, you can use 「に伴いまして」.
「危険を伴う」 and 「痛みを伴う」 use 「を伴う」, meaning “to involve, to come with”. That is different from this pattern.
The second half is usually an objective statement, not the speaker's personal intention or request.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on social change.
daily.example: With the falling birthrate, more and more elementary schools are closing.

daily.title: Building management notice
daily.description: The apartment office posts a water outage notice.
daily.example: Due to inspection work, the water will be shut off tomorrow.

work.title: HR announcement
work.description: HR announces an organizational change.
work.example: With the reorganization, department names will change.

work.title: Explaining a price change
work.description: Explaining to customers why prices are going up.
work.example: Due to the sharp rise in raw material costs, we will be revising our prices.

work.title: Market analysis
work.description: An analysis report describes an industry trend.
work.example: As the market expands, competition is also getting fiercer.

etymology: 「伴う（ともなう）」 comes from 「共（とも）」 “together” plus the suffix 「なう」, meaning “to accompany”. 「〜に伴って」 means “accompanying ...”: two things appearing together.

similar.title: 〜につれて
similar.explanation: Both express proportional change. 「につれて」 is more conversational and isn't used for one-time events; 「に伴って」 is more formal and can also mean “happening as a result of” (「移転に伴い」).

similar.title: 〜にしたがって
similar.explanation: 「にしたがって」 also expresses proportional change, and it can mean “to obey, to follow (rules)”. 「に伴って」 has no “obey” meaning.

similar.title: 〜とともに
similar.explanation: 「とともに」 can also mean “together with” or “at the same time as”; 「に伴って」 only expresses change or occurrence that comes along with something.

meaning: A strong assertion: “is nothing other than ..., is precisely ...”, stressing that it can't be anything else. Written language.
connection: Noun + にほかならない; plain form + から／ため + にほかならない

senses.label: Nothing but ...
senses.meaning: A strong statement that this is the true nature of something: “it is none other than ...”. Common in essays and speeches.
senses.connection: Noun + にほかならない; often with 「これは」 or 「〜とは」
examples: This success is nothing other than the result of everyone's hard work.
Education is nothing less than an investment in the future.
That is nothing but an excuse to avoid responsibility.

senses.label: Precisely because ...
senses.meaning: 「からにほかならない」 and 「ためにほかならない」 stress the reason: “the reason ... is precisely that ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + から／ため + にほかならない; often preceded by 「〜のは」
examples: The reason he passed is precisely that he studied every single day.
Parents are strict precisely because they love their children.

notes: Rare in everyday conversation. In speech, you can say 「まさに〜だ」 or 「〜こそ〜だ」.
「ほかならぬ + noun」 (「ほかならぬあなたの頼み」 “a request from none other than you”) is the noun-modifying form, without 「に」.
It can be written 「他ならない」 or 「外ならない」, but kana is more common today.

daily.title: Reading an editorial
daily.description: A newspaper column analyzes the cause of an accident.
daily.example: This accident was nothing other than a man-made disaster caused by lax management.

daily.title: Graduation ceremony
daily.description: The principal addresses the graduates.
daily.example: We have reached this day precisely because of our families' support.

work.title: Year-end speech
work.description: The president thanks all employees.
work.example: This term's strong results are nothing other than the hard work of every single employee.

work.title: Writing an academic paper
work.description: Arguing a conclusion in a paper.
work.example: This phenomenon can be considered nothing other than an effect of climate change.

etymology: 「ほか（外・他）」 means “other”, and 「ならない」 is the negative of the old copula 「なり」. 「Aにほかならない」 literally means “is not anything other than A”. The double negative strengthens the assertion: “it is precisely A”.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: 「にすぎない」 means “is merely ...” and sounds dismissive; 「にほかならない」 means “is precisely ...”, stressing the essence with no negative nuance.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: Both can emphasize a reason. 「からこそ」 is also common in speech; 「からにほかならない」 is more written and more assertive.

similar.title: 〜でしかない
similar.explanation: 「でしかない」 means “is only ..., nothing more” and gives a low evaluation; 「にほかならない」 confirms the true nature of something.

meaning: Shows the direction or target of an action or message (“toward ..., aimed at ...”), or preparation to achieve a goal (“in preparation for ...”).
connection: Noun + に向けて (to modify a noun: 「に向けた／に向けての + noun」)

senses.label: Toward / aimed at
senses.meaning: Shows the direction or target of an action or message: “to ..., toward ...”. Common with announcing, communicating, and departing.
senses.connection: Noun of target or place + に向けて; common in 「〜に向けて発信する」, 「〜に向けて出発する」
examples: The prime minister issued a message to the nation.
The ship left port bound for Tokyo.
We will strengthen our outreach aimed at young people overseas.

senses.label: Working toward a goal
senses.meaning: Acting to achieve a goal or to get ready for an upcoming moment: “in preparation for ..., toward ...”. The second half is usually preparation or effort.
senses.connection: Noun of goal, event, or time + に向けて; common in 「〜に向けて準備する」, 「〜の実現に向けて」
examples: I'm studying at the library every day to prepare for the exam.
Preparations are under way for hosting the Olympics.
Talks were held toward resolving the problem.

notes: To modify a noun, use 「に向けた + noun」 or 「に向けての + noun」. In mid-sentence, you can use 「に向け、」.
「子ども向けの本」 and 「初心者向け」 are noun + 「向け」, meaning “for (a target audience)”, without 「に」.
「に向かって」 focuses on physical direction or approach; 「に向けて」 is mostly for abstract goals and messages.

daily.title: Studying for a test
daily.description: Telling a friend what you've been up to.
daily.example: I'm memorizing vocabulary every night for next month's proficiency test.

daily.title: Club training camp
daily.description: Team members talk about practice before a match.
daily.example: The whole team is practicing hard for the tournament.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on a leader's speech.
daily.example: The president appealed to the world for peace.

work.title: Project meeting
work.description: The project lead confirms the team's goal.
work.example: Let's speed up development for next fiscal year's launch.

work.title: Presenting a strategy
work.description: A company introduces a new business direction.
work.example: We are developing a new product for overseas markets.

etymology: The transitive verb 「向ける（むける）」 means “to turn (something) toward”. 「〜に向けて」 originally meant “turning something toward a place”. From physical direction, it came to mean directing your efforts or attention toward a goal.

similar.title: 〜に向かって
similar.explanation: 「に向かって」 comes from an intransitive verb and stresses the subject moving toward or facing something; 「に向けて」 comes from a transitive verb and stresses directing actions or messages toward a target or goal.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: 「ために」 simply states a purpose; 「に向けて」 stresses step-by-step preparation for an upcoming goal.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: 「に対して」 marks the target of an action or a contrast; 「に向けて」 highlights direction and a goal.

meaning: “Depending on ..., in some cases ...”. Focuses on particular cases among several possibilities.

senses.label: Some ... will ...
senses.meaning: The first part is a factor that can vary (people, regions, situations, etc.). The second part describes a special result that happens in some of those cases: “some ... will ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + によっては; common in 「人によっては」, 「国によっては」, 「ところによっては」
examples: Some people may get sleepy from this medicine.
In some countries, tipping is customary.
Tomorrow, it may rain in some areas.

senses.label: Depending on the situation
senses.meaning: 「場合によっては」, 「状況によっては」, and 「結果によっては」 mean “depending on the situation, ... might happen”. Often used to warn in advance of possible serious consequences.
senses.connection: 場合・状況・結果・事情 etc. + によっては
examples: Depending on the situation, surgery may be necessary.
Depending on the results, we may also reconsider the plan.

notes: 「によって」 talks about the whole: “it differs depending on ...”. 「によっては」 focuses on just one special case.
The second half often pairs with 「〜こともある」, 「〜かもしれない」, or 「〜場合もある」.

daily.title: Weather forecast
daily.description: The forecaster describes the weather in different areas.
daily.example: There may be thunder in some areas.

daily.title: Talking about cultural differences
daily.description: Chatting with a foreign friend about Japanese food customs.
daily.example: In some regions, ozoni (New Year's soup) is made with miso.

work.title: Customer support
work.description: A support agent explains possible extra charges.
work.example: Depending on your application, additional fees may apply.

work.title: Internal meeting
work.description: A manager points out a project risk.
work.example: Depending on the situation, we will also consider postponing the project.

etymology: 「によって」 is the particle 「に」 plus the te-form of the verb 「因る（よる）」 “to depend on”. Adding the topic particle 「は」 singles out one particular case for emphasis.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: 「によって」 says the whole thing differs depending on ... (「人によって違う」); 「によっては」 talks about only some cases (「人によっては嫌がる」 “some people dislike it”).

similar.title: 〜次第だ・〜次第で (depending on)
similar.explanation: 「次第で」 stresses that the outcome depends entirely on the first part; 「によっては」 stresses that a special result occurs in some cases.

similar.title: 〜ようによっては
similar.explanation: 「ようによっては」 follows the masu-stem of a verb and means “if you look at it a different way” (「考えようによっては」); 「によっては」 follows nouns and expresses differing conditions.

meaning: Means “regardless of ..., irrespective of ...”, and can also mean “without relying on (a means)”. Written language.
connection: Noun + によらず (to modify a noun: 「によらない + noun」)

senses.label: Regardless of
senses.meaning: Not limited by the condition in the first part; it applies to everyone or everything: “regardless of ..., ...”. The first part is usually a category or attribute.
senses.connection: Noun + によらず; common in 「年齢・性別・経験によらず」, 「何事によらず」
examples: Anyone can take part, regardless of age or gender.
We hire capable people regardless of experience.
Whatever it is, it's important to see it through to the end.

senses.label: Without relying on
senses.meaning: Not using a certain means or method: “without resorting to ..., not through ...”.
senses.connection: Noun of means + によらず／によらない
examples: It should be resolved through dialogue, not by force.
I'm looking for a treatment that doesn't rely on medication.

senses.label: Unexpectedly
senses.meaning: The idiom 「見かけによらず」 means “contrary to appearances”. The proverb 「人は見かけによらない」 means “you can't judge a book by its cover”.
senses.connection: 見かけ + によらず／によらない
examples: He doesn't look it, but he's very strong.
You can't judge people by their looks.

notes: 「ず」 is the classical negative form. In speech, you can say 「〜に関係なく」.
To modify a noun, use 「によらない + noun」.

daily.title: Community event poster
daily.description: A poster explains who can join.
daily.example: Everyone is welcome to join, regardless of age.

daily.title: Complimenting a friend
daily.description: Surprised by an unexpected side of a friend.
daily.example: She doesn't look it, but she's a really good cook, isn't she?

work.title: HR policy
work.description: A company explains its evaluation policy.
work.example: At our company, we evaluate people on ability, not educational background.

work.title: International news
work.description: A report on the government's diplomatic stance.
work.example: The government is seeking a peaceful solution that doesn't rely on military force.

etymology: Made of the particle 「に」, 「よら」 (the irrealis form of the verb 「因る（よる）」), and the classical negative 「ず」. Literally “not depending on ...”. This gives the two meanings “regardless of ...” and “without relying on ...”.

similar.title: 〜を問わず
similar.explanation: Both mean “regardless of”. 「を問わず」 often follows paired words (「昼夜を問わず」 “day or night”, 「男女を問わず」 “men or women”); 「によらず」 can also mean “without relying on a means”.

similar.title: 〜にかかわらず
similar.explanation: 「にかかわらず」 often follows 「〜かどうか」 or two opposing items; 「によらず」 usually follows a single noun.

similar.title: 〜に限らず
similar.explanation: 「に限らず」 means “not limited to ...”, and the first part is included; 「によらず」 means “unrelated to ...”.

meaning: An action or state continues or extends over a whole range of time, space, or number of times: “for (a long period); throughout, across ...”.
connection: Noun of time・space・number range + にわたって (にわたり／にわたる + noun)

senses.label: Time span
senses.meaning: Continuing over a long period: “for ..., over the course of ...”. Stresses how long it lasts.
senses.connection: Noun of a period + にわたって; common in 「長年にわたって」, 「〜年にわたり」
examples: The meeting went on for five hours.
He has continued this research for 30 years.

senses.label: Area / field
senses.meaning: Spreading over a wide area or many fields: “throughout ..., covering ...”.
senses.connection: Noun of region or field + にわたって; common in 「全国にわたって」, 「多岐にわたる」, 「広範囲にわたる」
examples: The typhoon damage extended across the whole of Kyushu.
The topics range widely, from politics to economics.

senses.label: Number of times
senses.meaning: Done in several installments: “in ... parts, over ... rounds”.
senses.connection: Number + 回／度 + にわたって
examples: This program will be broadcast in three parts.
After several rounds of negotiation, they finally reached an agreement.

notes: To modify a noun, use 「にわたる + noun」 or 「にわたった + noun」. In mid-sentence, use 「にわたり」.
The first part is usually a long or wide range, stressing large scale. Small ranges like 「一日」 or 「一部屋」 are usually not used.
In 「アメリカに渡った」 (“crossed over to America”), 「渡る」 is the ordinary verb, not this grammar point.

daily.title: Weather forecast
daily.description: A forecast of rain over a wide area.
daily.example: Heavy rain is expected from the Kanto region to the Tohoku region.

daily.title: Reading a biography
daily.description: Describing a person's life.
daily.example: For half a century, she taught music to children.

work.title: Explaining a project
work.description: The project lead introduces a long-term plan.
work.example: This project is a long-term plan spanning three years.

work.title: Training notice
work.description: HR announces the training schedule.
work.example: New employee training will run for two weeks.

etymology: The verb 「渡る（わたる）」 originally means “to cross (a river or sea)”, and came to mean “to extend from one end to the other”. 「〜にわたって」 means continuing or spreading over a whole range. It can also be written 「亘る」, but kana is usual today.

similar.title: 〜を通して・〜を通じて
similar.explanation: 「を通して」 means “throughout the whole period” and can also mark a means; 「にわたって」 highlights a large range or scale.

similar.title: 〜から〜にかけて
similar.explanation: 「から〜にかけて」 gives a rough start and end, with fuzzy boundaries; 「にわたって」 stresses that the whole range is covered.

similar.title: 〜に至るまで
similar.explanation: 「に至るまで」 stresses that the range reaches all the way to an extreme endpoint; 「にわたって」 stresses the range as a whole.

meaning: Means “there's no need to ...” (often to politely decline or reassure someone), or “can't compare with, doesn't measure up to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form／noun + には及ばない

senses.label: No need to
senses.meaning: The matter isn't serious, so there's no need to do that. Often used to politely decline someone's concern or kindness. The polite form is 「には及びません」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form・action noun + には及ばない; common in 「ご心配には及びません」, 「わざわざ〜には及ばない」
examples: It's just a mild cold, so there's no need to worry.
You don't need to come all this way. A phone call is enough.
There's no need to apologize for something this small.

senses.label: Not as good as
senses.meaning: Ability or degree doesn't reach someone else's level. 「足元にも及ばない」 means “can't hold a candle to”.
senses.connection: Noun + には及ばない／にも及ばない
examples: My cooking is nowhere near as good as my mother's.
It's not at a professional level, but it's plenty good for a hobby.
Someone like me can't hold a candle to his talent.

notes: Meaning 1 is mostly used in formal situations. 「〜には及びません」 has a tone of polite refusal.
Meaning 1 can also be said without 「は」: 「〜に及ばない」.
「〜は言うに及ばず」 means “not to mention ...”. It's a separate set expression.

daily.title: Politely turning down an offer
daily.description: Declining when a friend wants to see you off.
daily.example: You don't need to see me off. The thought is enough.

daily.title: Talking about your idol
daily.description: Talking about the gap between you and someone great.
daily.example: No matter how much I practice, I'll never sing as well as he does.

work.title: Reassuring a client
work.description: An employee responds to a client worried about a malfunction.
work.example: We've already taken care of it, so there's no need to worry.

work.title: Replying modestly
work.description: Answering modestly when praised by your boss.
work.example: Oh no, I'm still nowhere near as good as my senior colleagues.

etymology: The verb 「及ぶ（およぶ）」 means “to reach, to extend to”. 「〜には及ばない」 literally means “doesn't reach ...”. For ability, it means “can't compare with”. For necessity, it means “things haven't reached the point of needing ...”, hence “no need to”.

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: Both mean “no need to”. 「までもない」 stresses that it's so obvious there's no need to go that far; 「には及ばない」 is mostly used to politely tell someone not to worry or trouble themselves.

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: 「ことはない」 is the conversational “there's no need”; 「には及ばない」 is more formal and polite.

similar.title: 〜は言うに及ばず
similar.explanation: 「言うに及ばず」 means “not to mention ...” and adds something further; 「には及ばない」 means “no need to” or “not as good as”.

meaning: Leaving something out: “without ..., minus ...”. Also “setting ... aside”.
connection: Noun + 抜きで／抜きの + noun; noun (+ は／を) + 抜きにして

senses.label: Without / minus
senses.meaning: Leaving out something normally included: “without ..., hold the ...”. Common when ordering food or talking about meals.
senses.connection: Noun + 抜きで／抜きの + noun; common in 「わさび抜き」, 「朝ご飯抜き」
examples: Excuse me, no wasabi, please.
I overslept this morning and left without breakfast.
I ordered coffee without sugar.

senses.label: Setting ... aside
senses.meaning: Putting something aside for now and not considering it. Common phrases: 「冗談は抜きにして」 (“joking aside”) and 「堅苦しい挨拶は抜きにして」 (“let's skip the formalities”).
senses.connection: Noun + は／を + 抜きにして
examples: Joking aside, I want you to think about it seriously.
Let's skip the formal greetings and get started.
Let's leave work talk out of it and just relax over a drink.

senses.label: Can't ... without
senses.meaning: 「〜抜きでは／抜きには〜ない」 means the second part can't happen without the first. It stresses that the first part is essential.
senses.connection: Noun + 抜きでは／抜きには + negative or expression of difficulty
examples: Without his cooperation, this project would not have succeeded.
You can't talk about Japanese summer festivals without mentioning fireworks.

notes: 「抜き」 is the noun form of the verb 「抜く」. 「手抜き」 (cutting corners), 「息抜き」 (a breather), and 「栓抜き」 (bottle opener) are compound nouns, not this grammar point.
Meaning 3 is close to 「〜なしには／〜なしでは」. 「抜き」 is a bit more conversational.

daily.title: Ordering at a sushi restaurant
daily.description: Ordering sushi without wasabi for a child.
daily.example: For the child's order, no wasabi, please.

daily.title: Party with friends
daily.description: Livening things up at the start of a get-together.
daily.example: Let's not hold back today and have fun.

daily.title: Talking about eating habits
daily.description: A friend talks about how they're dieting.
daily.example: Lately I've been skipping dinner.

work.title: At a meeting
work.description: A department head speaks at the start of a meeting.
work.example: Let's skip the preliminaries and get to the main topic.

work.title: Praising a team member
work.description: A manager acknowledges an employee's contribution.
work.example: Without Tanaka, we wouldn't have won this contract.

etymology: 「抜き」 is the stem of the verb 「抜く（ぬく）」 used as a noun. 「抜く」 originally means “to pull out, to remove”. 「〜抜きで」 means “with ... removed”, and 「抜きにして」 means “leaving ... out of the count”.

similar.title: 〜なしに(は)／〜なしでは
similar.explanation: Both can mean “without ...”. 「なしに」 is more written and can also follow action nouns: “do ... without doing ...”. 「抜きで」 focuses on deliberately leaving something out.

similar.title: 〜は別として
similar.explanation: 「は別として」 means “... is a separate matter”; 「は抜きにして」 means “setting ... aside” and is mostly used in set phrases.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: 「ずに」 follows verbs: “without doing ...”. 「抜きで」 follows nouns.

meaning: Attached to a verb, it means seeing a hard task through to the end, or doing something thoroughly, to the utmost.
connection: Verb masu-stem (drop ます) + 抜く

senses.label: See it through
senses.meaning: Overcoming difficulties and carrying on to the very end: “... to the end, ... all the way”. Mostly for things that take perseverance.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 抜く; common in 「やり抜く」, 「走り抜く」, 「戦い抜く」, 「生き抜く」, 「守り抜く」
examples: No matter how hard it gets, I intend to see it through to the end.
She ran the whole 42 kilometers to the finish.
I respect my grandfather, who survived hard times.

senses.label: Thoroughly / to the utmost
senses.meaning: Doing something very thoroughly, to the limit: “... thoroughly, ... long and hard”. Common with thinking, agonizing, and choosing.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 抜く; common in 「考え抜く」, 「悩み抜く」, 「選び抜く」, 「鍛え抜く」
examples: After thinking it through very carefully, I decided to quit my job.
We use only carefully selected ingredients.
I agonized long and hard before reaching this conclusion, so I have no regrets.

notes: 「追い抜く」 (to overtake), 「見抜く」 (to see through), and 「引き抜く」 (to pull out; to headhunt) are fixed compound verbs, not this grammar point.
Passive forms like 「選び抜かれた〜」 and 「鍛え抜かれた〜」 describe things that have been rigorously selected or trained.
Mostly attaches to volitional verbs, stressing a hard process or great intensity.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: Cheering up a friend who wants to give up.
daily.example: We've come this far, so let's keep going all the way to the end.

daily.title: Watching a sports match
daily.description: A commentator praises a player who played injured.
daily.example: Even though he was injured, he fought through the entire match.

daily.title: Reading product packaging
daily.description: A slogan on a tea package.
daily.example: We use tea leaves carefully selected by our artisans.

work.title: End of a project
work.description: A manager thanks the team.
work.example: Thank you for seeing this difficult project through to the end.

work.title: Presenting a proposal
work.description: The person in charge confidently presents a plan.
work.example: This proposal is the result of a lot of careful thought by our team.

etymology: The verb 「抜く（ぬく）」 originally means “to pull out, to pierce through”. After another verb, “piercing through to the other side” developed into “carrying an action all the way through” and “doing it to the utmost”.

similar.title: 〜きる・〜きれない
similar.explanation: 「きる」 stresses doing all of something, completely (「食べきる」 “eat it all”), focusing on the result; 「抜く」 stresses persevering through difficulties, focusing on the hard process.

similar.title: 〜通す
similar.explanation: 「通す」 stresses keeping the same state from start to finish (「黙り通す」 “stay silent throughout”, 「立ち通す」 “stand the whole time”); 「抜く」 stresses overcoming difficulties or reaching the utmost.

similar.title: 〜切る
similar.explanation: 「切る」 can also mean “extremely” (「疲れ切る」 “be exhausted”), mostly for states; 「抜く」 mostly follows volitional verbs and shows active perseverance.

meaning: Written language. “Not only ... but also ...”: the scope isn't limited to the first part but extends to the second.
connection: Noun／verb・い-adj. plain form + のみならず (な-adj. and noun predicates add 「である」)

senses.label: Not only ... but also
senses.meaning: The scope goes beyond the first part to include the second. The second part often uses 「も」 or 「まで」. Equivalent to 「だけでなく」, but more written and formal.
senses.connection: Noun + のみならず; verb・い-adj. plain form + のみならず; な-adj.・noun + である + のみならず
examples: This issue is important not only for Japan but for the whole world.
Not only can he speak English, he is also fluent in Chinese.
This town not only has convenient transportation but also abundant nature.

senses.label: At the start of a sentence: not only that
senses.meaning: Placed at the start of a sentence as a conjunction: “not only that, but ...”. Used in writing to add a further point.
senses.connection: Sentence 1。のみならず、sentence 2
examples: He was late for our appointment. Not only that, he didn't even apologize.

notes: With な-adjectives and noun predicates, add 「である」. You don't say ✕「便利のみならず」.
The emphatic forms 「ひとり〜のみならず」 and 「ただ〜のみならず」 are even more written.
In speech, 「〜だけでなく」 or 「〜ばかりでなく」 is enough.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on the effects of rising prices.
daily.example: Rising prices are affecting not only household budgets but also business management.

daily.title: Reading a travel guide
daily.description: A guidebook introduces an old temple.
daily.example: This temple is magnificent not only for its buildings but also for its garden.

work.title: Company profile
work.description: A company explains its management philosophy.
work.example: Our company values not only profit but also contributing to society.

work.title: Writing an academic paper
work.description: A paper explains the significance of the research.
work.example: The results of this study will benefit not only academia but also industry.

etymology: 「のみ」 is a classical restrictive particle (like 「だけ」 “only”), and 「ならず」 is the negative of the copula 「なり」. 「AのみならずB」 literally means “not only A”, which gives the meaning of adding something further.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「だけでなく」 works in both speech and writing; 「のみならず」 is written language and more formal.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: 「ばかりでなく」 is more conversational; 「のみならず」 is an objective, formal written way to add a point.

similar.title: 〜にとどまらず
similar.explanation: 「にとどまらず」 stresses going beyond a certain range (「国内にとどまらず海外にも」 “not just in Japan, but overseas too”); 「のみならず」 simply adds a point.

similar.title: 〜ひとり〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Adding 「ひとり」 stresses “not just this one ...”, and sounds even more formal.

meaning: Written language for limitation: “only, solely”. Similar to 「だけ」, but more formal.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + のみ; noun + particle (で・に・と) + のみ

senses.label: Only
senses.meaning: Limits the scope: “only ..., ... alone”. Common in notices, rules, news, and articles.
senses.connection: Noun + のみ; noun + particle + のみ (「日本でのみ」, 「ここにのみ」)
examples: This facility is for members only.
We accept cash only.
This product is sold only in Japan.

senses.label: All that's left is ...
senses.meaning: 「Verb dictionary form + のみだ」 means “the only thing left is to ...”. Often expresses determination, and sometimes resignation.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のみだ／のみです; common in 「あとは〜のみだ」, 「〜を待つのみ」
examples: All the preparations are done. Now all that's left is to wait for the real thing.
Now that we've come this far, the only thing to do is move forward.

notes: In speech, 「だけ」 is the norm. 「のみ」 is for writing or formal situations.
「〜のみならず」 means “not only ...” and is a separate grammar point.
Don't confuse it with 「飲み（のみ）」 “drinking”, as in 「飲み物」 or 「飲み会」.

daily.title: Reading a shop sign
daily.description: A sign at the entrance shows payment methods.
daily.example: Only cards are accepted at this store.

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: A report on a team reaching the final.
daily.example: Into the final. Now all that's left is to go for the title.

daily.title: Event poster
daily.description: A shopping mall explains a giveaway.
daily.example: Gifts for the first 100 customers only.

work.title: Access rules
work.description: A company explains who can edit a file.
work.example: Only administrators can edit this file.

work.title: Hiring notice
work.description: Explaining the selection process.
work.example: We will contact only those who pass the document screening.

etymology: 「のみ」 is a classical adverbial particle of limitation, equivalent to modern 「だけ」 or 「ばかり」. Today it survives mainly in written language and set expressions.

similar.title: 〜だけ
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「だけ」 works in any situation; 「のみ」 is more written and formal.

similar.title: 〜しか〜ない
similar.explanation: 「しか〜ない」 must pair with a negative and often feels like “not enough, too few”; 「のみ」 uses an affirmative form and sounds objective.

similar.title: 〜ただ〜のみ
similar.explanation: Adding 「ただ」 stresses “nothing but ...” and sounds stronger.

meaning: Doing something under someone's guidance, protection, or influence, or under a certain condition or in the name of something.
connection: Noun + のもとで／のもとに (in kanji: 「の下で」, 「の下に」)

senses.label: Under someone
senses.meaning: Under someone's guidance, care, or control: “under ..., in the care of ...”.
senses.connection: Person noun・guidance noun + のもとで; common in 「先生のもとで」, 「〜の指導の下で」, 「親のもとで」
examples: I did research under Professor Tanaka for three years.
He honed his skills under the guidance of a strict coach.
The child grew up healthy and strong in his parents' care.

senses.label: Under a condition
senses.meaning: Done under a certain condition, agreement, or system. Mostly written; 「のもとに」 is common.
senses.connection: Noun of condition, agreement, control, consent, etc. + のもとで／のもとに
examples: A new agreement was signed with the consent of both countries.
The experiment was carried out under strict control.
Personal information is used with the person's consent.

senses.label: In the name of
senses.meaning: 「〜の名のもとに」 means “in the name of ..., under the banner of ...”. Often has a critical tone.
senses.connection: Noun + の名のもとに
examples: Many people were hurt in the name of justice.
Many employees were laid off in the name of reform.

notes: When written 「〜の下で」, read it 「もと」, not 「した」. 「机の下（した）」 is a physical location, not this grammar point.
「のもとで」 focuses on doing something under an influence; 「のもとに」 is more written and common with conditions and names.
「〜をもとに」 means “based on ...”, which is different from 「のもとで」.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: An international student explains their research background.
daily.example: I am currently studying Japanese literature under Professor Yamada.

daily.title: Picnic outdoors
daily.description: Describing a picnic with friends.
daily.example: We all ate our bento under the blue sky.

daily.title: Reading a history book
daily.description: Reading about life under dictatorship.
daily.example: People were stripped of their freedom under the dictatorship.

work.title: Joint project
work.description: Explaining to a client how the partnership works.
work.example: With the cooperation of both companies, we are moving forward with new product development.

work.title: Data management
work.description: Explaining the rules for storing data.
work.example: The data is stored under strict control.

etymology: 「もと」 can be written 「下」, 「元」, or 「許」. Its original meaning is “base, root”, which came to mean “under ..., at the side of ...”. 「〜のもとで」 means “under ...”: being under someone's influence, control, or protection.

similar.title: 〜をもとに(して)
similar.explanation: 「をもとに」 means “using ... as material or a basis” (「事実をもとに書く」 “write based on facts”); 「のもとで」 means “under the influence or conditions of ...”.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: 「に基づいて」 means “based on (rules, data)”; 「のもとで」 means being under the control or protection of a person or condition.

similar.title: 〜の下（した）で
similar.explanation: In 「机の下で」 it's read 「した」 and means the physical space below; 「のもとで」 is the abstract “under the influence or control of”.
